reference.source: RCOG postpartum haemorrhage guidance / Williams Obstetrics
clinicalPearls: Uterine atony is failure of the myometrium to contract and retract adequately after delivery, and it is the single commonest cause of primary postpartum haemorrhage

Effective haemostasis after birth depends on myometrial contraction compressing the spiral arteries of the placental bed (the 'living ligatures'); when the uterus stays relaxed these vessels bleed freely
Within the 'four Ts' framework of postpartum haemorrhage (Tone, Trauma, Tissue, Thrombin), atony is the 'Tone' cause and should be excluded first, though causes may coexist

Risk factors include overdistension from multiple pregnancy, polyhydramnios, or macrosomia, prolonged or augmented labour, precipitate labour, grand multiparity, chorioamnionitis, retained placental tissue, tocolytic use, and general anaesthesia with volatile agents
The classic finding is a soft, poorly contracted, often high uterus with ongoing vaginal bleeding despite a delivered and apparently complete placenta

First-line management is uterine massage and bimanual compression, ensuring the bladder is empty, and uterotonic drugs such as oxytocin, ergometrine, prostaglandins, and misoprostol, alongside resuscitation

If pharmacological measures fail, mechanical and surgical options include intrauterine balloon tamponade, compression sutures such as the B-Lynch, stepwise uterine and internal iliac artery ligation, uterine artery embolisation, and ultimately hysterectomy
Prophylactic active management of the third stage with a uterotonic markedly reduces the incidence of atonic postpartum haemorrhage
reference.pathophysiology: After the placenta separates, the large uteroplacental blood flow must be arrested rapidly. This is achieved mechanically by contraction and retraction of the interlacing myometrial fibres, which constrict the spiral arteries traversing them, with clotting a secondary contributor. Uterine atony occurs when the myometrium fails to maintain this tonic contraction. Overdistension stretches and fatigues the fibres; prolonged or augmented labour and chorioamnionitis impair contractility; retained tissue mechanically prevents full retraction; and certain drugs, such as tocolytics and volatile anaesthetics, relax smooth muscle. With the vessels left open and uncompressed, blood loss is brisk and can rapidly become life-threatening given the high uterine blood flow at term.
additionalDifferentials: Genital tract trauma such as cervical, vaginal, or perineal lacerations or a haematoma
Coagulopathy, inherited or acquired, including disseminated intravascular coagulation
additionalInvestigations: Assessment of uterine tone by palpation and the response to massage
Estimation and ongoing measurement of blood loss with serial maternal observations
Full blood count, coagulation screen with fibrinogen, and group-and-save or crossmatch
Inspection of the placenta for completeness and examination of the genital tract for trauma
Bedside ultrasound to detect retained tissue if bleeding persists
Near-patient viscoelastic testing where available to guide blood-product replacement
redFlags: Continuing heavy bleeding with a soft, poorly contracted uterus
Signs of hypovolaemic shock such as tachycardia, hypotension, or altered consciousness
Failure to respond to first-line uterotonics
Developing coagulopathy or a need for massive transfusion
Bleeding out of keeping with the visible loss, suggesting concealed or intra-abdominal haemorrhage
reference.prognosis: With early recognition and a structured escalation of uterotonic, mechanical, and surgical measures, most women recover fully; however, atonic postpartum haemorrhage remains a leading cause of maternal death worldwide, and delayed treatment risks shock, coagulopathy, organ injury, and loss of fertility from hysterectomy.
pitfalls: Failing to give a prophylactic uterotonic in the third stage
Not emptying the bladder, which impairs uterine contraction
Attributing ongoing bleeding to atony without excluding trauma, retained tissue, and coagulopathy
Underestimating blood loss and escalating too slowly
Neglecting to keep the patient warm and correct coagulopathy during resuscitation
references: RCOG Green-top Guideline on prevention and management of postpartum haemorrhage
WHO recommendations on the prevention and treatment of postpartum haemorrhage
management: Immediate uterine massage and bimanual compression with the bladder emptied as first-line mechanical measures
Stepwise uterotonic drugs including oxytocin, ergometrine, prostaglandins such as carboprost, and misoprostol
Concurrent resuscitation with wide-bore intravenous access, crystalloid and blood-product transfusion guided by ongoing loss and coagulation results
Exclusion and treatment of coexisting causes within the four Ts framework, including retained tissue, genital tract trauma and coagulopathy
Escalation to intrauterine balloon tamponade, uterine compression sutures, and uterine artery or internal iliac ligation or arterial embolisation if bleeding persists
Hysterectomy as a life-saving last resort with senior obstetric, anaesthetic and haematology involvement
